title: Symmetries and Conservation
intro: An observable that commutes with the Hamiltonian is conserved: its expectation value, and its whole probability distribution, never change. This page introduces the Heisenberg picture, where that statement is natural, and the Z-parity symmetry of the QRC spin reservoir.

blocks.text: Expectation values can be computed by moving the state or by moving the observable:

blocks.caption: Schrödinger picture on the left, Heisenberg picture on the right. They always agree.

blocks.text: In the Heisenberg picture the state stays put and the operators evolve, obeying $\tfrac{d}{dt}A(t) = i[H, A(t)]$. This is the natural picture for a reservoir: the readout measures fixed observables $Z_i$ at different times, which is the same as measuring the initial state with the moving observables $Z_i(t)$. Virtual nodes are exactly a set of such Heisenberg-evolved observables (Readout and Multiplexing (#/qrc/models/readout-and-multiplexing)).

If $[H, Q] = 0$, the equation of motion gives $\tfrac{d}{dt}Q(t) = 0$: $Q$ is conserved. More than its average is fixed: $H$ and $Q$ share an eigenbasis, $U(t)$ maps each eigenspace of $Q$ to itself, and the probability of every outcome of $Q$ is constant. The space splits into blocks (symmetry sectors) that never talk to each other.

Energy itself is always conserved under a time-independent $H$. Other examples: total $Z$ (the number of excitations) for flip-flop couplings $X_iX_j + Y_iY_j$, which move an excitation without creating or destroying any; and for a Hamiltonian built only from $X_iX_j$ and $Z_i$, the parity $\Pi = Z_1Z_2\cdots Z_n$.
The parity of the reservoir Hamiltonian

Each $X_iX_j$ anticommutes with $Z_i$ and with $Z_j$ and commutes with every other $Z$, so it commutes with the product of all of them (two sign flips cancel). Each $Z_i$ commutes with $\Pi$ trivially. So the Fujii–Nakajima Hamiltonian $\sum J_{ij}X_iX_j + \sum h_iZ_i$ conserves $\Pi$: XX couplings create or destroy excitations only in pairs, so whether the count is even or odd never changes. The $2^n$-dimensional space splits into two blocks of $2^{n-1}$.

This has consequences you can see on the QRC shelf. Level statistics must be computed within one block (Dynamical Regimes (#/qrc/models/dynamical-regimes)); an input written into the parity-odd coherences is invisible to parity-even readouts such as $Z_i$ (Input Encoding (#/qrc/models/input-encoding)); and in the special case $h = 0$ extra conserved quantities appear that stop the reservoir forgetting its initial state (Contraction and Fixed Points (#/qrc/open-systems/contraction-and-fixed-points)).

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import expm
X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], complex); Y = np.array([[0, -1j], [1j, 0]]); Z = np.diag([1., -1.]).astype(complex)
def op(o, i, n):
    m = np.eye(1)
    for k in range(n): m = np.kron(m, o if k == i else np.eye(2))
    return m
n = 3; rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
# The reservoir Hamiltonian of the QRC shelf: random XX couplings plus a Z field
H = sum(rng.uniform(-.5, .5) * op(X, i, n) @ op(X, j, n) for i in range(n) for j in range(i + 1, n))
H = H + sum(op(Z, i, n) for i in range(n))
parity = op(Z, 0, n) @ op(Z, 1, n) @ op(Z, 2, n)
comm = lambda A, B: A @ B - B @ A
print("[H, Z1 Z2 Z3] = 0:", np.allclose(comm(H, parity), 0), "   [H, Z1] = 0:", np.allclose(comm(H, op(Z, 0, n)), 0))
# Heisenberg picture: <Z1>(t) computed both ways
psi = np.zeros(8, complex); psi[0b100] = 1          # |100>: qubit 1 excited
U = expm(-1j * H * 1.3)
schr = np.vdot(U @ psi, op(Z, 0, n) @ (U @ psi)).real
heis = np.vdot(psi, (U.conj().T @ op(Z, 0, n) @ U) @ psi).real
print(f"<Z1>(t=1.3): Schrodinger {schr:+.4f}, Heisenberg {heis:+.4f}")
print(f"parity <Z1Z2Z3> at t=0 and t=1.3: {np.vdot(psi, parity @ psi).real:+.0f}, {np.vdot(U @ psi, parity @ (U @ psi)).real:+.0f}")
# XX + YY conserves total Z (excitation number); XX alone does not
Hflip = op(X, 0, 2) @ op(X, 1, 2) + op(Y, 0, 2) @ op(Y, 1, 2); Ztot = op(Z, 0, 2) + op(Z, 1, 2)
print("[XX+YY, Z1+Z2] = 0:", np.allclose(comm(Hflip, Ztot), 0), "   [XX, Z1+Z2] = 0:", np.allclose(comm(op(X, 0, 2) @ op(X, 1, 2), Ztot), 0))

blocks.text: Output of the run: for a random 3-qubit reservoir Hamiltonian, $[H, Z_1Z_2Z_3] = 0$ but $[H, Z_1] \ne 0$. Starting from $\vert100\rangle$, $\langle Z_1\rangle$ at $t = 1.3$ is $-0.6494$ in both pictures, while the parity stays at $-1$. Flip-flop coupling $XX + YY$ conserves $Z_1 + Z_2$; $XX$ alone does not.

Conserved quantities as 'fixed points in disguise' that break the echo state property: Contraction and Fixed Points (#/qrc/open-systems/contraction-and-fixed-points).
Integrable and localised Hamiltonians have many conserved quantities, which is what makes them poor reservoirs: Dynamical Regimes (#/qrc/models/dynamical-regimes).

blocks.title: Does parity commute with a coupling?
solution: $Z_1Z_2X_1X_2 = (Z_1X_1)(Z_2X_2)$, since operators on different qubits commute.
blocks.answer: Yes: the two minus signs cancel

blocks.title: Where can an excitation go?
blocks.text: Two qubits evolve under $J(X_1X_2 + Y_1Y_2)$ and start in $\vert01\rangle$. Which basis states can ever have non-zero amplitude?
solution: The coupling conserves $Z_1 + Z_2$, which is 0 for $\vert01\rangle$ and $\vert10\rangle$, $+2$ for $\vert00\rangle$ and $-2$ for $\vert11\rangle$.
So the state stays in the span of $\vert01\rangle$ and $\vert10\rangle$: the excitation hops between the qubits but is never created or lost.

blocks.title: A conserved quantity and a readout
blocks.text: A reservoir Hamiltonian conserves $Z_1Z_2Z_3$, and the initial state is $\vert000\rangle$ with no input. Express $\langle Z_1Z_2\rangle$ in terms of a single-qubit feature.
solution: The state stays in the parity $+1$ block, where $Z_1Z_2Z_3 = 1$ on every basis state.
Multiplying by $Z_3$ (with $Z_3^2 = I$): $Z_1Z_2 = Z_3$ on that block, so $\langle Z_1Z_2\rangle = \langle Z_3\rangle$ at all times.
